solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Condone stripping sexy American in church

indicators.note: to strip something is to peel off its outer covering, so only the inside letters survive

parts.note: the word with its first and last letters peeled away

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another means it is placed inside it

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
US is the standard short form for American

explanation.surface: Someone tolerates a striptease by a sexy American performed inside a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stripping' looks like a striptease but tells you to remove the outside of the next word. CE, the Church of England, is the commonest crossword church.
explanation.definitionFit: To excuse a fault is to pardon or overlook it, which is what condoning means.

clue.text: Detachment of militiamen eagerly knocked back constipation remedy

indicators.note: knocking back a drink tips it backwards, so the letters run in the opposite direction
a detachment is a part split off from a larger unit, so the answer is a part of the following words

parts.note: the letters straddling the two words, read in clue order

explanation.surface: A unit of militiamen eagerly downs a laxative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Detachment' sounds military to suit the militiamen, but it means a piece cut from the words. Read militiAMEN Eagerly backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: An enema flushes the bowel with injected liquid and is a classic treatment for being blocked up.

clue.text: Old king's entertaining on subject of languages

indicators.note: a host entertaining guests has them inside the house, so one piece holds another

parts.note: Old King Cole of the nursery rhyme, with the possessive S
RE means 'on the subject of', as in a letter heading

explanation.surface: An ancient monarch holds forth on the topic of languages.
explanation.walkthrough: Old King Cole is the 'merry old soul' of the nursery rhyme; his name with 's wraps around RE.
explanation.definitionFit: A creole is a full language formed from the mixing of two or more tongues, so creoles are languages.

clue.text: Mutant Daleks orbiting perimeter of devastated Earth? Flee!

indicators.note: to orbit is to circle around something, so one piece goes round another
a mutant has changed form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
E is the abbreviation for Earth

indicators.note: a perimeter is the boundary of an area, so only the outside letters are taken

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A Doctor Who alarm: mutated Daleks circle a ruined Earth, so run!
explanation.walkthrough: Daleks are the alien villains of the British TV series Doctor Who; Earth supplies its abbreviation and joins the shuffle, while 'devastated' contributes only its edges.
explanation.definitionFit: Skedaddle is a colloquial verb meaning run away hurriedly, so as a command it says the same as flee.

clue.text: Smell of fish on Sabbath

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing on another is placed after it

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for Sabbath
a tench is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: The whiff of fish cooked on a Sunday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smell of fish' reads as one phrase, but 'of' only joins definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A stench is a strong, unpleasant odour, a particularly foul kind of smell.

clue.text: Doctrine that can be read both ways

indicators.note: a word reading identically forwards and backwards is what reading both ways describes

parts.note: the meaning: a principle or belief held as true; the word for it is the same read in either direction

explanation.surface: A dogma open to two interpretations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Read both ways' suggests an ambiguous belief, but it means the word spells the same backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenet is a principle or belief held by a group, the same thing as a doctrine.

clue.text: Foster child turned up outside university lesson on heroin

indicators.note: in a down clue, one thing on another sits above it, so the second comes after
one piece sits outside another, wrapping around it
in a down clue, turning something up flips it so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: a son is a child
U is the abbreviation for university
RI is religious instruction, a school lesson
H is slang for heroin

explanation.surface: A foster child has gone to the bad, with a university lesson on heroin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foster child' looks like a single phrase, but 'Foster' is the definition and 'child' starts the wordplay. NOS wraps U and RI, then H follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To foster growth or development is to nourish it, both meaning to feed and encourage.

clue.text: Roll these out for guest

indicators.note: out means wrong or disordered, so the letters are set in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Roll out the welcome for a visitor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roll out' reads as a phrasal verb, but 'Roll' is fodder and only 'out' signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A hosteller is a person who stays at a hostel, a type of paying visitor or lodger.

clue.text: Zulu renegade initially spurned by extremely juvenile floosy

indicators.note: spurning rejects something, and initially points at the first letter as the one rejected
by means beside, so the pieces are placed next to each other
the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only those letters are taken

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
Zulu is Z in the NATO phonetic alphabet
a renegade is a rebel; drop its first letter

explanation.surface: A Zulu rebel is rejected by a very young good-time girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially spurned' sounds like the rebel being rejected by the girl, but it only removes the first letter of the renegade's synonym. Zulu stands for Z in the radio alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Jezebel, from the biblical queen, is a by-word for a shameless or immoral woman, as is a floosy.

clue.text: Poles kept apart in remarkably quiet hearing

indicators.note: items kept apart inside something are placed separately within it
something remarkable is out of the ordinary, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written
N and S are the north and south poles

explanation.surface: Polish people are segregated at an unusually silent court session.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' looks like people from Poland but means the two magnetic poles, N and S, which go into the rearranged QUIET at separate points.
explanation.definitionFit: An inquest is a judicial inquiry, usually into a death, held as a formal hearing.

clue.text: Blankets tangled round a plant stem

indicators.note: going round something encloses it, so one piece wraps another
tangled things are twisted out of order, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Bedcovers have got twisted around a houseplant's stalk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blankets' looks like the definition, but it is the letters to shuffle; the single A sits inside them.
explanation.definitionFit: A beanstalk is the long climbing stalk of a bean plant, a particular kind of plant stem.

clue.text: Standard complaint involving international ruling body

parts.note: par is the standard or normal level

indicators.note: to involve something is to include it, so one piece takes another inside

parts.note: a lament is an expression of grief or complaint
I is the abbreviation for international

explanation.surface: The usual grievance about an international governing organisation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standard complaint' reads as a routine moan, but the two words are separate pieces, and the international abbreviation slips into the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A parliament is the elected assembly that makes a nation's laws, so it is a governing body.

clue.text: Gift seems oddly superfluous object

indicators.note: if the odd-numbered letters are surplus, they are thrown away and the even ones kept

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: A present that strangely appears to be an unnecessary thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' usually means keep the odd letters; here 'superfluous' says the odd ones are the extras to discard.
explanation.definitionFit: An item is a single thing or article, the same as an object in the everyday sense.

clue.text: Some of those deviants like men in tights!

indicators.note: taking some of a phrase means using only a part of its letters

parts.note: the letters spanning the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: A sneer at oddballs who fancy men in tights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like' reads as a verb of fancying, but it belongs to the definition, meaning 'similar to'. The answer runs across tHOSE Deviants.
explanation.definitionFit: Hose is an old word for tights or stockings, so someone wearing hose is dressed as men in tights were.

clue.text: Thugs ultimately rough soldier up in dodgy saloon

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is taken

parts.note: the final letter of the word

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from the bottom, backwards
one piece sitting in another is placed inside it
something dodgy is unreliable or crooked, so the letters are put in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
a GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: Thugs eventually beat up a soldier in a shady bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rough soldier up' reads as beating him up, but 'rough' gives only its end and 'up' flips the soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: Hooligans are violent, rowdy troublemakers, exactly the kind of people called thugs.

clue.text: Beasts rushed around lobbies heartlessly pursuing women

indicators.note: to pursue is to follow behind, so one piece comes after the other
turning around faces the other way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: ran is the past tense of run, to rush

indicators.note: without a heart means the central letter is taken out

parts.note: W is the abbreviation for women
halls are entrance lobbies; remove the middle letter

explanation.surface: Brutes dash about the corridors, cruelly chasing women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartlessly' seems to describe the brutes' cruelty, but it removes the centre of the word for lobbies.
explanation.definitionFit: Narwhals are tusked Arctic whales, so they are animals, which is what beasts means.

clue.text: Pagan priest laid bare country's bankruptcy

indicators.note: laying something bare strips off its outer covering, so the inner letters are kept

parts.note: a druid is a Celtic pagan priest; lose its first and last letters
a nation is a country; the 's is just 'is'

explanation.surface: A heathen holy man exposed a nation's financial collapse.
explanation.walkthrough: The priest is a DRUID, the ancient Celtic priest, stripped of its outer letters before the country follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruination is the state of being ruined, and financial ruin is what bankruptcy amounts to.

clue.text: Sacrificed sheep close to kitchen within stronghold

indicators.note: within means inside, so these pieces go inside another

parts.note: a fort is a stronghold
a ewe is a female sheep

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so its last letter is taken

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A sheep was sacrificed near the kitchen inside a castle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sacrificed sheep' looks like a slaughtered animal, but 'Sacrificed' is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Forewent is the past tense of forgo, meaning gave something up, which is what sacrificed means.

clue.text: Book time off, lying about pressing danger essentially

indicators.note: to press into something is to push inside it, so one piece is squeezed into another
something lying about is turned round, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: leave is time off work

indicators.note: the essence of a thing is at its core, so only the central letters are taken

parts.note: the two central letters of the word

explanation.surface: Someone books holiday, lying about an urgent danger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book' looks like a verb for reserving time off, but it is the noun definition. 'Pressing' sounds like 'urgent', but here it means pushing in.
explanation.definitionFit: An evangel is a gospel, one of the four books of Christ's life in the New Testament.

clue.text: Presume speaker's wearing ermine?

indicators.note: what a speaker gives is heard rather than read, so the sound matters, not the spelling

parts.note: ermine is a white fur, so wearing it puts you in fur

explanation.surface: Assume the orator is dressed in ermine, like a judge or peer.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that ermine is an example of fur rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: To infer is to reach a conclusion from evidence, close to presuming or supposing something.

clue.text: Cloth covering Spooner's pet's point of access?

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts trade places

parts.note: a cat's small door; swap the starting sounds of the two words

explanation.surface: A cloth that covers the little door the pet uses to get in.
explanation.walkthrough: A cat flap is a small hinged door for a pet. A flat cap is the soft, peaked cloth cap associated with northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat cap is a soft woollen or tweed cap, so it is a head covering made of cloth.

clue.text: Detective starts to search area in Tuscan province

parts.note: a PI is a private investigator

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, so only the opening letters are taken

parts.note: the first letter of each word

explanation.surface: A detective begins searching a district of Tuscany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' reads as part of the search scene but only joins wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Pisa, famous for its leaning tower, is the city that gives its name to a province of Tuscany in Italy.

clue.text: Bear east of British port before a storm

indicators.note: in an across clue, east is to the right, so this piece comes after
coming before means placed ahead of the next piece

parts.note: Hull is a port city in Yorkshire, England
taken as written
Baloo is the bear in Kipling's The Jungle Book

explanation.surface: A bear on the coast east of a British harbour ahead of a gale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear' looks like a verb meaning endure, but it is a named bear. 'Storm' is a storm of protest, not weather.
explanation.definitionFit: A hullabaloo is a noisy commotion or uproar, the same as a storm of fuss or outrage.

clue.text: Underworld figure seen regularly in cheap dress

indicators.note: something seen at regular intervals appears every other step, so alternate letters are kept

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: A gangster often spotted in a cheap frock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Underworld figure' suggests a mobster, but it is the Greek god of the dead.
explanation.definitionFit: Hades is the Greek god who rules the realm of the dead, a mythical ruler below the earth.

clue.text: Landlady sparing daughter from dispiriting event

indicators.note: to spare someone from something is to leave them out of it, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: a downer is something depressing
D is the abbreviation for daughter; it is removed

explanation.surface: A landlady spares her daughter a depressing occasion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sparing' sounds kind, but it means removing the letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A landlady is the woman who owns a property and rents it out, so she is its owner.

clue.text: Poorly-dressed model leaves play hugging German

indicators.note: to hug is to hold in your arms, so one piece wraps around another
when something leaves, it departs, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: a tragedy is a kind of play
the Model T was Ford's early car; it is removed
G is the abbreviation for German

explanation.surface: A shabbily dressed model walks out of a show, embracing a German.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' looks like a fashion model but is the Ford Model T, giving one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Raggedy describes someone in tattered, worn-out clothes, which is how a poorly dressed person looks.

clue.text: Digging up stuff about Charlie acting effeminately

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: mining digs ore out of the ground
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Raking up gossip about a man called Charlie who behaves camply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digging up stuff' suggests scandal-raking, but it is literal extraction from the earth.
explanation.definitionFit: To mince is to walk with affected, dainty steps, a stereotyped way of behaving effeminately.

clue.text: Get wet cat onto evacuated ship

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece onto another is attached after it
an evacuated building has its contents emptied, so only the outer letters stay

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
the cat o' nine tails is a whip, so a cat is a lash

explanation.surface: A cat climbing onto an abandoned ship gets soaked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cat' looks like the animal, but it is the cat o' nine tails, a whip used for flogging sailors.
explanation.definitionFit: To splash someone is to throw or spatter liquid over them, making them wet.

clue.text: Rifleman pins back English beside river

indicators.note: beside means next to, so the pieces are placed side by side
going back means running in the opposite direction, so the letters reverse

parts.note: taken as written
E is the abbreviation for English
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A gunman pins back an Englishman by the riverside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pins back' looks like restraining someone, but 'back' simply turns the word round.
explanation.definitionFit: A sniper is a marksman with a rifle who shoots from hiding, a particular kind of rifleman.
